source.title_on_document: EEG assessment of artificial intelligence-generated content impact on student creative performance and neurophysiological states in product design

supplement.holds: Not specified in the saved PDF. The data availability statement says original contributions are included in the article/Supplementary material, but identifies no supplementary file, table, or statistic (p. 14). The PDF ends with references and contains no appended supplement. Direct requests to the stated Frontiers article and the DOI URL were blocked by network permissions, so supplementary contents remain unverified.

paper_design_summary: At a university design laboratory in Eastern China, 64 third-year undergraduate design students used either AIGC tools or traditional design tools for a three-hour intelligent walking-cane task (p. 4, Sections 3.1 and 3.2.2; pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2.3 and 3.4). Section 3.1 explicitly states random assignment, although Section 3.2.1 calls the design quasi-experimental (p. 4). Three design experts scored the submitted designs using the Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale, while EEG concentration and relaxation and post-task interviews measured the design process (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2.3 and 3.3; p. 10, Section 3.8).

studies.label: Intelligent walking-cane design with AIGC versus traditional tools

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were assigned to the experimental AIGC group or the traditional-design control group. The statement of random assignment to conditions is distinct from the cluster random sampling used for recruitment. The randomization procedure is not described, and the separate quasi-experimental label is an internal inconsistency.
assignment.quote: They were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (n = 32; 17 females, 15 males) or the control group (n = 32; 16 females, 16 males).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1 Participants (random assignment); p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Research variables (conflicting quasi-experimental label); p. 4, Section 3.2.2 and p. 5, Section 3.2.3 (controlled laboratory sessions).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is stated in the supplied article; methods are on pp. 4-7.

arms.name: Experimental group (AIGC)
arms.description: ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion were available during design. The described workflow used ChatGPT for concepts and refinement, Stable Diffusion for design images, and Photoshop or Illustrator for post-processing (p. 4, Section 3.2.2; p. 6, Section 3.4.2). Counts at assignment: p. 4, Section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

arms.name: Control group (traditional tools)
arms.description: Participants researched literature and existing products via the internet, sketched by hand or with CAD software, modeled in Rhinoceros, rendered in KeyShot, and used Photoshop/Illustrator for post-processing; Autodesk Maya is also listed among available conventional tools. No AIGC assistance (p. 4, Section 3.2.2; p. 6, Section 3.4.3). Counts at assignment: p. 4, Section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The assignment paragraph gives 32 students per arm, and Table 1 analyzes 32 per arm; the paper does not explicitly describe an intention-to-treat analysis (p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 8, Table 1).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduates in Product Design and Visual Communication Design at a public university, all enrolled in a Design Innovation course. Recruitment occurred in the Spring semester of 2024 (March to June). Participants had foundational design and modeling coursework but no prior formal training using AIGC tools for design (p. 4, Section 3.1).
participants.quote: The study included a total of 64 participants, with 32 in the experimental group and 32 in the control group.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1 Participants (recruitment, country, random assignment and arm counts); p. 7, Section 3.7 Quantitative analysis results (quoted analyzed counts); p. 8, Table 1 (analyzed counts).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion; specific model/version identifiers are not stated (p. 4, Section 3.2.2).
ai_tool.how_used: A combined chatbot and image-generation workflow: students engaged in multiple rounds of ChatGPT dialogue about functions, interaction methods, technology, inspiration, examples, and optimization; then generated and iterated design images with Stable Diffusion before conventional image editing. Midjourney is named in the equipment list and illustrated in interview accounts. The role code records image generation; open-chat ideation/refinement was also part of the intervention (p. 4, Section 3.2.2; p. 6, Section 3.4.2; p. 11, Table 3).

task.description: Design an intelligent walking cane for elderly people or people with mobility impairments, considering functionality, intelligent features, ergonomics, aesthetics, innovation, and sustainability. Required deliverables were design sketches, three-dimensional models, and rendered images (p. 6, Section 3.4.1).

outcomes.name: Creative performance: Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (CSDS)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three design-field experts independently scored participants' submitted creative works with the CSDS. The scale has 30 five-point items covering Relevance and Effectiveness, Novelty, Elegance, and Genesis; the paper describes weighted-average dimension scores and a possible creative-performance score of 150 (pp. 5-6, Section 3.3.1). Only the overall creative-performance score is reported by arm, with one analyzed score per participant; no separate dimension estimates are given (p. 8, Table 1; p. 9, Table 2). Aggregation across the three raters and rater blinding are not specified. Creative performance is RQ1, but the paper does not explicitly designate a primary outcome (p. 2, research questions). Figures 4 and 5 display the same creative-performance outcome and its relationships with EEG measures, rather than additional creativity outcomes (pp. 9-10).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group M = 115.13, SD = 6.440, N = 32; control group M = 110.69, SD = 9.372, N = 32 (Table 1). Mean difference = 4.438; 95% confidence interval of difference: lower 0.419, upper 8.456 (Table 2). t(62) = 2.208, p = 0.031 (Section 3.7); Cohen's d = 0.55 (Section 4.1). Table 2 prints 2.208 under df and 62 under t; the prose explicitly identifies t(62) = 2.208.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 1 and Section 3.7; p. 9, Table 2; pp. 10-11, Section 4.1. Control's internet research and conventional design aids: p. 6, Section 3.4.3.

sample_overlap.locator: No sample sharing or reanalysis is stated; p. 4, Section 3.1 describes recruitment for the present study.

company_involvement.description: No company author, named corporate funder, or company research role is reported. Author affiliations are academic. Funding lists educational and institutional programs, including university-industry and industry-federation programs, but names no individual company; the authors declare no commercial or financial relationships constituting a potential conflict of interest.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; p. 14, Funding and Conflict of interest.

eligibility.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly reports random assignment of students to AIGC assistance versus traditional tools (p. 4); this supports lab_rct coding despite Section 3.2.1's contradictory quasi-experimental label. The experiment was conducted in controlled university laboratory sessions (p. 4, Section 3.2.2; p. 5, Section 3.2.3). Table 1 reports 64 people analyzed, with 32 per arm, exceeding the 50-person threshold (p. 8). Design experts scored the students' actual submitted designs with the CSDS (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2.3 and 3.3.1). AI was used while those designs were produced (p. 6, Section 3.4.2), so the outcome answers with_ai; there is no separate unassisted post-AI creative task.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted students had higher expert-rated creative-performance scores than traditional-tool students (M = 115.13 versus 110.69; n = 32 per arm; p = 0.031; Cohen's d = 0.55; p. 8, Table 1 and Section 3.7; p. 11, Section 4.1).
open_questions: The explicit random-assignment statement in p. 4, Section 3.1 conflicts with the quasi-experimental label in Section 3.2.1; the allocation procedure is not described. This form follows the explicit assignment statement.

The separate supplement is referenced on p. 14 but is not included in the supplied PDF. Its contents and any additional output outcomes or statistics remain unverified because both the Frontiers and DOI requests were blocked by network permissions.
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. The complete supplied markdown and all 15 PDF pages, including all tables and figures and the references, were read. Outcome inventory: Tables 1-2 (pp. 8-9) report CSDS creative performance, EEG concentration, and EEG relaxation; Figures 4-5 (pp. 9-10) visualize these same measures and their correlations. Table 3 (p. 11) reports interview themes of concentration state, design idea development, creative process experience, technical challenges, time management, and perceived control. Figure 1 (p. 5) describes the procedure and these three quantitative assessments; Figures 2-3 (pp. 7-8) show example design works without additional outcome scores. Only creative performance is scored on the produced output and enters the outcomes array. EEG measures and interview experiences are outside the three screening questions. The four CSDS dimensions are described as scale components, but no dimension-specific results are reported. No between-person output-diversity measure or creative output produced after AI removal is reported. The contrast is coded ai_vs_active because the control explicitly uses internet research and conventional CAD, rendering, and image-processing aids (p. 6, Section 3.4.3). Outcome timing reflects when the design was produced, even though experts rated it afterward (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2.3 and 3.4). The t and df headings in Table 2 are reversed relative to the clearly labeled prose; the form preserves the printed values and identifies the discrepancy. No effect size or standard error was calculated. The data availability statement points generally to the article/Supplementary material and correspondence, without a separate data repository or code URL (p. 14).
